blurb: The classic hot-pink yarrow: broad flat corymbs packed with hundreds of tiny cerise-magenta florets, each one lit by a pale cream-white eye, riding above a low mat of ferny grey-green foliage from June into September. Bone-dry tough, deer-proof and mobbed by bees. But be honest about that colour — it is at its cherry-cerise best the day a floret opens and drifts steadily paler, dustier and finally brown from there, and the Chicago Botanic Garden's four-year yarrow trial gave 'Cerise Queen' its lowest rating for exactly that plus a sprawling, flopping habit. Grown lean, deadheaded hard, and bought in bloom, it is still the brightest pink in a xeric bed.
size: ~2–2.5 ft tall in bloom (25–32 in. measured over four seasons in the Chicago trial) × 2 ft and widening — a spreading plant, not a tidy clump
sun: Full sun — 6+ hours of direct sun; less and the stems stretch, lean and flop
water: Low; xeric once established — no supplemental water in an average Front Range summer, and overwatering is the surest way to flatten or rot it
spread: Spreads steadily by rhizome and self-sows; rated a spreading, flopping habit in the Chicago trial, where 18–24 in. gaps had closed by the second season — give it lean ground, an edge, and a division every 2–3 years
seasons: Ferny grey-green foliage pushing from an overwintering basal rosette in spring; flat cerise corymbs from June into September, each head drifting paler and then brown as it ages; stems are usually cut back after frost, so winter presence is slight
wildlife: The flat corymbs are an easy landing pad — native bees, hoverflies, beneficial wasps and butterflies work them hard; an RHS 'Plants for Pollinators' selection, and yarrow carries Xerces Society recognition for special value to native pollinators
deer: Deer- and rabbit-resistant — the bitter, aromatic ferny foliage is left alone
toxic: Toxic to dogs, cats and horses if eaten (achillein, monoterpenes, achillin); the foliage causes allergic contact dermatitis in sensitive people and prolonged contact can raise the skin's photosensitivity — wear gloves
origin: A European garden selection of the Eurasian Achillea millefolium complex, whose pink and red garden forms were bred and introduced from Europe; the wild species itself is far-flung across Europe, temperate Asia and most of temperate North America, Colorado included
habitat: Lean, well-drained grassland, meadow, roadside and open disturbed ground — dry to average soils in full sun

care.hardiness: Cold is a non-issue here: common yarrow and its cultivars are rated USDA 3–9, and the RHS gives 'Cerise Queen' its top H7 rating, hardy below −20 °C.[3][4][6] Boulder's zone 5b–6a winters are well inside that, and the Chicago Botanic Garden's four-year Achillea trial found cold hardiness was not a limiting factor for the millefolium cultivars.[1] What limits this plant on the Front Range is not winter but summer — heat and age wash the cerise out of the flowers, and rich or shaded ground makes the stems collapse.[1][4][8]
care.planting: Set container plants out any time in the growing season; spring after the mid-May last frost or early September gives the roots the kindest weeks, and bare-root divisions are best planted in spring.[9] Site it in full sun on the leanest, sharpest-draining ground you have — resist the usual reflex to dig in a barrow of compost, because fertile soil is precisely what makes yarrow run and flop.[4][8] The RHS lists it for chalk, loam and sand (not clay) and asks for well-drained soil, so on Boulder's heavy clay work in coarse grit or plant it on a berm or raised edge.[3] In a pot it looks good for a season, but the rhizomes fill the container fast and roots in pots are far less cold-hardy than in-ground crowns — sink the pot or move it somewhere sheltered for winter, and plan to knock it out and divide it every spring.[4][9]
care.sun: Full sun, 6 or more hours of direct sun a day.[6] Our high-altitude light is not the problem — shade is: in anything less than full sun the stems stretch, relax and end up on the ground, and flower production drops.[4][8] The Chicago trial plots got 8–10 hours of sun a day and 'Cerise Queen' still flopped, so treat full sun as the floor, not the fix.[1]
care.soil: Lean, dry-to-medium, well-drained ground is what it wants; it tolerates poor soils as long as drainage is good.[4] Alkalinity is not a concern — NC State gives it a soil pH range of about 6.0–8.0, the RHS lists it for acid, neutral and alkaline soils, and the Chicago trial ran on soil measured at pH 7.6, right in Front-Range territory.[1][3][6] Do not enrich it. Overly fertile soils produce rapidly spreading plants that flop, and moist, rich soil is the single most reliable way to turn a 2-ft plant into a sprawling mat of brown stems.[4][8]
care.water: Genuinely xeric. It is drought-tolerant once established, rated dry-to-medium at Missouri Botanical Garden, described as extremely drought resistant by Clemson, and listed by PlantTalk Colorado among the water-wise perennials for sun in this climate.[4][7][10] Water it properly through the establishment season — CSU suggests new full-sun plantings often need water every couple of days for the first month, stretching to every four to six days after that — and then essentially stop.[9] In an ordinary Boulder summer it needs nothing extra; in a brutal July a deep soak every two or three weeks is the most it should ever get. Too much water is what kills it, by root rot in wet soil and by lush stems that lodge.[4][6]
care.spacing: Space plants 18–24 in. apart — the Chicago trial planted its yarrows at 46–61 cm (18–24 in.) and the interplanting space had closed by the second season.[1] Clemson suggests a tighter 12–18 in., but on good ground you will only be dividing sooner, so err wide.[7] Leave a real gap to whatever it neighbours, and expect to spade around the edge each spring: this is a plant that fills its allotment and then some.[1][4]
care.propagation: Division in spring is the method.[3] CSU names yarrow specifically among the mid-to-late-summer and fall bloomers that should be divided in spring before growth begins — lift the clump, cut away the woody, thinning centre, and replant the vigorous outer pieces with roots attached.[9] Do it every 2–3 years to maintain vigour and flowering.[4][7] Basal cuttings taken in early summer also root readily. What will not work is seed: 'Cerise Queen' is a named clone, and seed-raised Achillea strains are notoriously unreliable — the Chicago evaluators marked their seed-grown entries down for mixed flower colours, variable form, plant size and foliage, calling the uncertainty of the actual flower-colour mix a negative attribute.[1] Because seed-grown 'Cerise Queen' is widely sold, buy a plant in flower or take a division from a clone whose colour you have actually seen, rather than sowing and hoping.[1][3]
care.bloom: Expect flowers from early June through late August, and with deadheading on into September — the Chicago trial recorded 'Cerise Queen' as early June to late August, Missouri Botanical Garden and NC State give June to September for the species, and the RHS puts it in summer and autumn.[1][3][4][6] Peak bloom typically arrives about a month after the first flowers open.[1] The colour is the whole point and the whole problem: fresh florets are a deep cerise-magenta (matched to RHS colour chart 71C in the trial) with a pale eye, but colours faded as the flowers aged, with several colour gradations visible on a plant at once.[1][3] 'Cerise Queen' was singled out as one of two cultivars that required deadheading immediately as flowers faded, or the spent flowers quickly turned brown.[1] Missouri Botanical Garden says the same of its sibling red cultivar 'Paprika' — initial flower colour fades, sometimes rather quickly, to light pink, creamy yellow and brown.[5] Plan on cutting spent heads every few days in July if you want a clean cerise display rather than a dusty one.
care.feeding: Don't. Overly fertile soils result in rapidly spreading plants that tend to flop, and moist, rich ground produces the weak stems that lodge.[4][8] The Chicago trial fed its plots just once a year, a slow-release granular in May at one pound per 100 square feet, and even that was on nursery-standard beds.[1] On a typical amended Front-Range bed, skip fertilizer entirely; on genuinely sterile fill you might give one light spring topdressing of compost and nothing more.
care.maintenance: Deadhead relentlessly — cut spent heads the moment the colour goes, or they brown on the plant and drag the whole display down.[1] Shearing the plant back by roughly a third to a half after the main flush both limits height and prompts a second wave; Missouri Botanical Garden recommends cutting stems back in late spring and again after flowering to reduce sprawl.[4] If it leans anyway, a grow-through hoop set in late spring is easier than tying up a collapsed clump in August, but the real cure is lean soil and full sun.[1][4][8] Cut back after frost (the Chicago trial cut its plots each autumn and top-dressed with 2–3 in. of mulch for winter), though CSU now recommends lighter fall cutback for overwintering pollinators except where pest or disease is present.[1][9] Then lift, edge or divide the rhizomes every 2–3 years before the centre thins.[4][7]
care.troubles: Disease is minor. Powdery mildew and a fungal infection of the flower buds were the only diseases observed across the whole four-year Chicago trial, and mildew was worst on the A. ptarmica group rather than the millefolium cultivars.[1] Missouri Botanical Garden adds occasional stem rot and rust, plus weak stems that lodge easily; NC State notes root rot in soils kept too wet, and contact dermatitis from handling.[4][6] In practice, almost every failure on the Front Range is a siting decision rather than a pathogen: too much water, too much fertility or too much shade gives a floppy, fast-running plant, while the other common disappointment — a muddy, washed-out pink instead of cerise — is the cultivar behaving exactly as trialled, not a nutrient problem.[1][4][5][8]
care.companions: Put it in the driest, leanest, sunniest zone and give it neighbours that want the same irrigation — Russian sage, lavender, catmint, penstemon, blanket flower, prairie zinnia, blue grama and little bluestem — which is CSU's hydro-zoning idea applied at bed scale, and keeps you from watering the yarrow to death on someone else's schedule.[9][10] The cerise reads beautifully against silver foliage and blue-violet spikes. Missouri Botanical Garden puts common yarrow in cottage gardens, meadows, prairies and naturalized areas and warns it is generally too aggressive for a formal border, which is fair — give it a wild-edged planting rather than a manicured one.[4] It is also a first-rate cut flower fresh and one of the best yarrows for drying.[1][2]

edible.card: Young leaves & flowers — bitter tea/seasoning, tiny amounts only
edible.summary: Yarrow leaf and flower have a long, documented use as a bitter tea and seasoning herb — the European Medicines Agency licenses yarrow herb as a traditional herbal tea for loss of appetite and mild digestive complaints — but it is a small-dose herb with real contraindications, not a salad green, and this particular plant is an ornamental bedding cultivar selected for flower colour.[11][12]
edible.parts: The edible parts are the leaves and the flowers, taken from the aerial growth — the EMA monograph covers Millefolii herba, the dried flowering aerial parts, and the flowers separately, prepared as herbal tea.[12] The Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center records the long-standing use of yarrow leaf tea for digestive complaints among Native American peoples.[11] Everything is strongly bitter and aromatic, so the quantity anyone actually uses is small — a few young leaves as a seasoning, or a cup of tea.[11][12]
edible.preparation: Pick young leaves in spring before the plant flowers, when they are tenderest and least resinous, and use only a few, chopped fine, as a bitter seasoning; flowers and dried leaves are steeped as a tea.[11][12] The EMA's traditional preparations are simply the comminuted dried herb as a herbal infusion, taken for a short period, with advice to see a doctor if symptoms persist beyond about two weeks.[12] Treat any tasting of a garden cultivar as a curiosity in small amounts: 'Cerise Queen' was bred and evaluated for flower colour and garden performance, never for flavour or food use.[1][6]
edible.caution: Read this before eating any of it. (1) Allergy. The EMA contraindicates yarrow outright for anyone hypersensitive to yarrow or to other plants of the Asteraceae (Compositae) family — ragweed, chamomile, daisies — and allergic skin reactions to yarrow medicines are documented.[12][13] (2) Skin and light. Allergic contact dermatitis from yarrow has been described since 1899; the sesquiterpene lactone α-peroxyachifolid is a confirmed strong sensitizer, and cross-reaction with other Compositae is well recorded.[13] UC ANR warns that in rare cases yarrow causes severe allergic skin rashes and that prolonged exposure can increase the skin's photosensitivity, advising gloves, long sleeves and long trousers when working with it.[14] (3) Thujone. Yarrow's volatile oil can contain α- and β-thujone, a known neurotoxin on oral intake; the EMA concluded the amounts in properly prepared yarrow tea are too low to present a risk, but that finding covers a controlled tea dose, not eating quantities of leaf, and thujone content varies enormously between plants.[12][13] (4) Pregnancy, nursing and children. Safety in pregnancy and lactation has not been established and the EMA does not recommend its use then; yarrow is additionally reputed to be an abortifacient and to affect the menstrual cycle, and yarrow medicines are not for anyone under 12.[12][13] (5) THE ID WARNING — this is the one that kills people. Yarrow's finely dissected, lacy foliage is exactly what makes foragers confuse it with deadly members of the carrot family. Alabama Extension makes the comparison directly: yarrow is a 1–3 ft sunflower-family plant with hairy, finely divided leaves oval-to-elongated in outline, whereas poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*) is a 3–10 ft carrot-family plant with large, glossy, triangular, fern-like leaves, smooth hairless purple-splotched stems and a musty odour — and its alkaloids depress the central nervous system to paralysis of heart and lungs, then death.[16] Poison hemlock is a Colorado List C noxious weed and is common on Front-Range ditchbanks and disturbed ground.[18] Western water hemlock (*Cicuta*) is worse still — described by OSU Extension as the most violently toxic of all North American plants, with a piece of root the size of a walnut enough to kill a 1,200-lb cow.[17] Never eat a lacy-leaved plant you have not positively identified; harvest only from a plant you deliberately planted and can name. (6) Pets. The ASPCA lists yarrow as toxic to dogs, cats and horses — glycoalkaloids (achillein), monoterpenes and sesquiterpene lactones (achillin) — with vomiting, diarrhoea, colic, drooling, anorexia, dermatitis and depression.[15] (7) Nursery chemicals. Ornamental yarrows are sold as bedding and border stock and are routinely treated with pesticides in production; never eat a plant fresh from the garden centre, and never eat a plant you have sprayed.[6]
